```{r setup}
library(mbmm)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

auc <- function(score, positive) {
  r <- rank(score)
  np <- sum(positive)
  nn <- sum(!positive)
  (sum(r[positive]) - np * (np + 1) / 2) / (np * nn)
}
```

## What this vignette must establish

**Scientific question:** does a baseline covariate change the probability of
productive infection?

**Why MBMM:** productive infection is latent. A participant can have a
transient detectable measurement without the sustained viral trajectory that
defines the biological state.

**Route I:** an independent sample of known productively infected donors is
available. Its trajectories define the state-1 kinetic population. The
analysis participants never contribute to that bank.

Because this is a simulation, we know the true state and the true gate
coefficient. Success means that MBMM should:

1. distinguish productive infection better than an "any detection" rule;
2. recover the negative direction and approximate size of the gate effect;
3. preserve uncertainty for ambiguous participants; and
4. reject the no-covariate gate in a permutation test.

The simulation is deliberately larger than a toy example. A small donor bank
is not expected to reproduce a smooth generating population atom by atom;
the scientific checks concern held-out state evidence and the gate effect.

## The hierarchy in scientific language

| MBMM object | Meaning in this simulation |
|---|---|
| $Y_i$ | repeated, possibly censored viral-load measurements |
| $Z_i=1$ | productive infection |
| $Z_i=0$ | no productive infection; some participants have transient detections |
| $x_i$ | standardised baseline covariate |
| $\Pr(Z_i=1\mid x_i)$ | logistic gate with true slope $-1.5$ |
| $G_1$ | kinetic population estimated from independent state-1 donors |
| $L_{i1}$ | analysis trajectory integrated over $G_1$ |
| $L_{i0}$ | background likelihood near the assay floor |

The covariate enters only the gate. It is not used to build the bank or to
score trajectories.

## Mechanistic trajectory: the eclipse-phase viral ODE

The productive-infection candidates solve

\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot T &= -\beta T V,\\
\dot I_1 &= \beta T V-\kappa I_1,\\
\dot I_2 &= \kappa I_1-\delta I_2,\\
\dot V &= pI_2-cV.
\end{aligned}
\]

$T$ is susceptible target cells, $I_1$ and $I_2$ are eclipse and productive
infected cells, and $V$ is viral load. A candidate row supplies the kinetic
parameters. `eclipse_trajectory()` solves this system; `eclipse_design()`
constructs an identifiable candidate design.

```{r simulate, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
analysis <- simulate_mbmm(n = 160, beta_ab = -1.5, prevalence = 0.3,
                          p_abortive = 0.4, n_pool = 120, seed = 7)

reference <- simulate_mbmm(n = 360, beta_ab = 0, prevalence = 0.5,
                           p_abortive = 0, n_pool = 120, seed = 17)
reference_ids <- reference$truth$id[reference$truth$z == 1]
reference_obs <- subset(reference$obs, id %in% reference_ids)

c(analysis_participants = nrow(analysis$truth),
  independent_state1_donors = length(reference_ids))
```

The reference simulation is generated independently, contains no abortive
state-0 records, and is then restricted by the known simulated state. That
restriction is what makes the donor bank *pure*. Independence alone would not
be enough if the donor set were an unrestricted state mixture.

```{r observed-trajectories, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE), echo = FALSE, fig.alt="Twelve simulated viral-load trajectories split by true productive-infection state; sustained high curves occur primarily in state 1."}
plot_ids <- unlist(lapply(split(analysis$truth$id, analysis$truth$z), head, 6))
plot_obs <- subset(analysis$obs, id %in% plot_ids)
plot_obs$plot_value <- ifelse(plot_obs$censored, plot_obs$lod,
                              plot_obs$value)
plot_obs$state <- factor(analysis$truth$z[match(plot_obs$id, analysis$truth$id)],
                         levels = 0:1,
                         labels = c("State 0: not productive",
                                    "State 1: productive"))

ggplot(plot_obs, aes(time, plot_value, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = censored), size = 1.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~state) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 16, `TRUE` = 2),
                     labels = c(`FALSE` = "Observed",
                                `TRUE` = "Censored at assay limit")) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Viral load (log scale)",
       shape = "Censored",
       title = "Longitudinal records carry more information than any detection",
       caption = "Triangles are left-censored values displayed at their assay limit.")
```

For visualisation only, a censored value is drawn at its assay limit and marked
with a triangle. The likelihood does **not** treat it as an observed value at
that limit: `trajectory_loglik()` uses the appropriate left-tail probability.

## Build the state-1 bank from independent donors

First create candidates and reject any trajectory that becomes non-positive
between visits. This is a mechanistic screen fixed without the analysis
cohort.

```{r candidates, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
candidates <- eclipse_design(500, seed = 2)

trajectory <- function(time, theta) {
  eclipse_trajectory(time, theta$beta, theta$delta, theta$p, theta$V0,
                     kappa = theta$kappa, c_clear = theta$c_clear,
                     T0 = theta$T0)
}

positive <- screen_positive(candidates, trajectory,
                            grid = seq(0, 22, by = 0.5))
candidates <- positive$candidates
c(rejected_nonpositive = positive$rejected,
  retained_positive = nrow(candidates))
```

`trajectory_loglik()` evaluates every donor against every candidate under a
log-scale Gaussian observation model with exact handling of left censoring.
The generating residual scale is known here to be 0.5.

```{r reference-likelihood, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
LL_reference <- trajectory_loglik(reference_obs, candidates, trajectory,
                                  sigma = 0.5)

screen <- screen_candidates(LL_reference, nu = 80)
bank_candidates <- candidates[screen$keep, , drop = FALSE]
bank <- fit_bank(LL_reference[, screen$keep, drop = FALSE], lambda = 1)

c(candidate_atoms = nrow(bank_candidates),
  effective_atoms = 1 / sum(bank$weights^2))
```

The candidate support screen uses only independent donors, so it is also
independent of every scored analysis participant. `fit_bank()` estimates how
frequently those kinetic candidates occur in the donor population.

## Form the two class likelihoods

```{r class-likelihoods, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
LL_analysis <- trajectory_loglik(analysis$obs, bank_candidates, trajectory,
                                 sigma = 0.5)
l1 <- class_loglik(LL_analysis, bank$weights)
l0 <- background_loglik(analysis$obs, sigma = 0.5, floor = 0.5)
```

For state 1, `class_loglik()` integrates rather than selects across the bank.
For state 0, `background_loglik()` represents repeated measurements near the
assay floor. No infection-time lag is integrated here because
`simulate_mbmm()` generated observations without a latent timing offset. A
real analysis should integrate a lag only when that uncertainty belongs to
its observation model.

## Fit the covariate gate

```{r gate, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
X <- cbind(intercept = 1, baseline = analysis$truth$x)
fit <- fit_gate(l1, l0, X)
oracle <- coef(glm(z ~ x, data = analysis$truth, family = binomial()))

coefficient_check <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("Generating truth", "Oracle using true state", "MBMM"),
  intercept = c(analysis$alpha, oracle[1], fit$gamma[1]),
  baseline_slope = c(-1.5, oracle[2], fit$gamma[2])
)
coefficient_check
```

The oracle is the ordinary logistic fit that would be available if productive
infection were observed without error. It separates finite-sample variation
in the simulated states from error introduced by latent-state inference.

```{r responsibility-plot, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE), echo = FALSE, fig.alt="Posterior productive-infection probabilities grouped by known simulated state, with intermediate values showing uncertainty."}
plot_responsibility(fit, analysis$truth$z) +
  labs(title = "Posterior responsibility compared with the known state",
       subtitle = "Intermediate values retain genuine classification uncertainty")
```

```{r gate-plot, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE), echo = FALSE, fig.alt="Estimated and true productive-infection probabilities decrease with the baseline covariate along similar curves."}
plot_gate(fit, analysis$truth$x, truth = analysis$truth$z,
          true_probability = plogis(analysis$alpha -
                                    1.5 * analysis$truth$x)) +
  labs(x = "Baseline covariate", y = "Probability of productive infection",
       title = "The inferred gate follows the generating gate")
```

## Did MBMM recover what it should?

```{r recovery, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
detected <- tapply(!analysis$obs$censored, analysis$obs$id, any)

recovery <- c(
  true_slope = -1.5,
  oracle_slope = unname(oracle[2]),
  mbmm_slope = unname(fit$gamma[2]),
  mbmm_state_AUC = auc(fit$w, analysis$truth$z == 1),
  detection_rule_AUC = auc(as.numeric(detected), analysis$truth$z == 1),
  uncertain_responsibilities = sum(fit$w > 0.1 & fit$w < 0.9)
)
round(recovery, 3)
```

```{r detection-table, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
table(any_detection = detected, true_productive_state = analysis$truth$z)
```

```{r permutation-test, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
test <- gate_test(l1, l0, X, B = 199, seed = 1)
test
```

These executable checks prevent the vignette from quietly presenting a failed
simulation as success.

```{r executable-checks, eval = requireNamespace("deSolve", quietly = TRUE)}
stopifnot(
  recovery["mbmm_state_AUC"] > 0.85,
  recovery["mbmm_state_AUC"] > recovery["detection_rule_AUC"],
  recovery["mbmm_slope"] < 0,
  abs(recovery["mbmm_slope"] - recovery["oracle_slope"]) < 1,
  recovery["uncertain_responsibilities"] > 0,
  test$p_value <= 0.05
)
```

## What this example establishes—and what it does not

In this controlled setting, an independent, pure state-1 donor bank produces
useful held-out state evidence, outperforms thresholded detection, and recovers
the gate effect. It checks the package's Route I computation against known
truth.

For a real study, the user must still justify donor-state purity,
transportability of within-state kinetics, candidate coverage, the observation
model, and the complete independence of bank construction. Return to the
[scientific and practical guide](mbmm.html), or continue to the
[Route II simulation](sdy2354.html) to see how the construction changes when
no labelled reference population exists.
